result.summary: Pausanias describes the river Helisson and the sights of Megalopolis: temples, statues and porticoes in and around the market-place. He pauses to praise Polybius, the historian whose statue stands there.

scenes.title: The river Helisson
scenes.summary: The river's course is traced and shown to divide Megalopolis in two. A temple of Watching Poseidon stands near the city.

scenes.title: Precinct of Lycæan Zeus
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the temple of Lycæan Zeus, the statues of Pan and Apollo, and the ruined temple of the Mother of the Gods.

scenes.title: Porticoes and public offices
scenes.summary: Philip's portico, the temple of Hermes, the magistrates' offices and the Myropolis portico are described.

scenes.title: Statue of Polybius
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statue of Polybius and praises his history and his service to the Greeks under Rome.

scenes.title: Temple of Zeus Soter
scenes.summary: The Aristandreum and the temple of Zeus Soter are described, with statues by Cephisodotus and Xenophon.

alias_notes.explanation: Pan's surname, from the Nymph Œnoe who nursed him.
Title taken from the hill Scolitas in Megalopolis.
Honorific name of Scipio after the African war.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias credits Polybius's advice with Roman success and ignoring it with disaster.

analysis.text: Pausanias reads the city through its monuments, noting decay, lost statues and borrowed names.
The praise of Polybius reflects Greek acceptance of Roman rule and the Achæan League's role under it.

fun_facts.text: The Helisson divided Megalopolis, a city founded in the 4th century BC, much as channels split Cnidos and Mitylene.

language_notes.text: "Watching Poseidon" translates the cult title Hippokourios/Phytalmios? Uncertain; here it simply names a cult epithet meaning the god as watcher or guardian.
"No approach to it" means the shrine was closed to entry, though its interior could be seen from outside.
Œnois is a surname derived from the Nymph Œnoe; "privately" suggests she nursed Pan in secret or personally.
Epicurius means "helper" or "succourer", an epithet of Apollo, explained later by Pausanias in his account of Phigalia.
An elegiac couplet is a two-line verse form of a hexameter and a pentameter, commonly used for inscriptions.
Philip the son of Amyntas is Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great; the Megalopolitans honoured him by naming the portico after him.
Acacesius is a cult title of Hermes, probably meaning 'the one who does no harm' or 'averter of evil'.
A cubit is an ancient measure, roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches; so the Pan is a small figure.
Myropolis means roughly 'perfume-seller's place', suggesting the portico was a market for unguents; the name is not explained in the text.
Elegiac verses are poems in alternating long and short lines (couplets), the usual form for inscriptions.
Rased is an old spelling of razed, meaning levelled to the ground.
The Achæan League was a federation of Greek cities; after Rome's conquest in 146 BC Polybius helped arrange their settlement.
Artemis Preserver translates the cult title Soteira, parallel to Zeus Soter, 'Saviour'.

context_notes.text: Cnidos and Mitylene were Greek cities, on the Asia Minor coast and on Lesbos, each divided by a channel of water.
Lycæan Zeus was worshipped on Mount Lycæum in Arcadia, the region's most ancient and revered cult of Zeus.
Megalopolis was founded around 370 BC as a new Arcadian capital, and nearby cities contributed to adorn it.
Bassæ, near Phigalia, was the site of a famous temple of Apollo.
Diophanes of Megalopolis was an Achæan League leader, father of the general Diæus's line; the League united much of the Peloponnese.
Pan, the goat-footed god of shepherds, was especially honoured in Arcadia, where Megalopolis lay.
Polybius of Megalopolis (c. 200–118 BC) was a Greek statesman and historian, son of Lycortas, an Achæan League leader.
Cephisodotus and Xenophon were Athenian sculptors of the early fourth century BC; Pentelic marble came from Mount Pentelicus near Athens.

literary_notes.text: The surviving head alone conveys decay and loss, suggesting the fragmentary state of the city's monuments.
Absent statues and bare bases continue the motif of ruin, with empty pedestals standing as evidence of lost glory.
A temple reduced to a stone tortoise leaves a poignant contrast between the god's former honour and present ruin.
Polybius is presented as a wise adviser whose counsel decided outcomes, building his authority through cause and effect.
